data.author: Elis Gjevori

Khamenei says Iran will push enemy forces out of Arabian Sea
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned enemy forces that they will soon lose their foothold in the Arabian Sea, after saying Iranian fighters had forced them away from the country’s southern waters, state media reported.
“Having suffered painful blows from our valiant combatants and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they [the enemy] dare not venture beyond the Arabian Sea,” he said.
“Whenever they have risked doing so, they have only inflicted harm upon themselves; and the time is fast approaching when the Arabian Sea, too, will be cleared of their presence.”
His message marked Sacred Defence Week, which commemorates the Iran-Iraq War, and the anniversary of former Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah’s killing in 2024.

data.author: MEE correspondent
data.summary:
On hope: What Iranians hold on to in uncertain times
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on

As war, economic pressure and instability make long-term plans harder, Iranians are still finding ways to enjoy the present and build a future they can no longer clearly see
Women react to bubbles as they walk at the Grand Bazaar in Tehran on 30 March 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off
Velayat Park, south of Tehran, was already crowded before dawn on a September morning as hundreds of runners gathered for a 10-kilometre race.
People arrived in groups or alone. Music played as runners waited, talking, laughing and preparing for the competition. The women's race went first.
In their running gear, many women wore sports head coverings provided at the event. Others, however, ran with their hair uncovered. Videos of the race soon circulated widely online, turning the event into a national talking point. The authorities later announced legal proceedings against the organisers over violations of Iran’s mandatory dress rules.
But for the runners themselves, at least for those interviewed for this story by Middle East Eye, that morning was about something more ordinary: just running.
Fahimeh, a psychologist who took part in the race, described the atmosphere as a rare experience of energy, hope and life. She was struck by the energy and enthusiasm of the people who had come together in the early hours of 18 September.
Her description of hope was simple: "It did not mean believing that everything would be better tomorrow. It meant making a choice today."
That choice is difficult to understand without looking at what has happened to Iran's sense of the future in recent years.
The impact of two wars in consecutive years, and the possibility of another round of military conflict, have become deeply visible in everyday life. data.title: Middle East Eye: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
For more than two decades, Iraq's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York.
The arrangement, created after the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction.
Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran.
The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups.
Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds.

A faded union jack was still fluttering defiantly over the British Consulate in the troubled Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in East Jerusalem this morning.
The door of the consulate was open for business as usual. But there is uncertainty over how much longer that will be the case.
No more than ten days are left before it closes, if Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar has his way.
Three weeks ago Saar announced the closure of the consulate as part of a package of retaliatory measures following UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements. He gave a deadline of 8 October.
It has been widely assumed that Britain would comply with this Israeli order, but Middle East Eye can reveal this is not certain.
Today, this reporter received an evasive response when we approached the Foreign Office asking for confirmation that Britain would close the consulate.
We understand that, although a final decision has not yet been made, Britain may be pondering whether to defy the Israeli ultimatum.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel chokes West Bank movement amid Jewish holiday
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Israel chokes West Bank movement amid Jewish holiday
Israeli forces have stepped up restrictions on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, blocking roads, limiting movement and causing hours-long waits at checkpoints.
The army has blocked entrances to several towns and villages with iron gates and earth mounds, including on secondary roads, since the Jewish holiday of Sukkot began on 25 September.
Checkpoints have also been tightened across the territory, as a comprehensive closure of the West Bank is set to remain in place until the holiday ends on 3 October.
The Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints north of Ramallah, along with the Jaba’ checkpoint northeast of Jerusalem, stand out as prominent examples of checkpoints characterised by long waiting times, particularly during peak hours.
These checkpoints slow the movement of Palestinians between villages, towns and cities, with delays often extending further depending on inspection procedures and conditions at the site, thereby creating major bottlenecks on routes used daily by thousands of Palestinians.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran denies involvement in suspected plot targeting UK airbase
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Iran denies involvement in suspected plot targeting UK airbase
Iran’s embassy in the UK has “categorically” rejected and condemned speculation linking Tehran to a suspected plot targeting a UK military airbase used by the United States.
The embassy said the claims were “unfounded and malicious” and criticised British individuals and media outlets for attempting to link Iran to the incident at RAF Fairford.
The embassy also threatened legal action to “safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people” over what it described as misleading and damaging media reports.
UK counterterrorism police said five men, all UK nationals in their mid-20s, had been arrested in connection with the incident.

Roadblocks and checkpoints delay Palestinians and hamper ambulance crews reaching patients
People sit on a sofa with a waterpipe to watch as commuters wait in their vehicles at the Israeli Atara checkpoint on Route 465 near Ramallah, occupied West Bank, 27 September 2026 (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
Off
Israeli forces have stepped up restrictions on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, blocking roads, limiting movement and causing hours-long waits at checkpoints.
The army has blocked entrances to several towns and villages with iron gates and earth mounds, including on secondary roads, since the Jewish holiday of Sukkot began on 25 September.
Checkpoints have also been tightened across the territory, as a comprehensive closure of the West Bank is set to remain in place until the holiday ends on 3 October.
The Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints north of Ramallah, along with the Jaba’ checkpoint northeast of Jerusalem, stand out as prominent examples of checkpoints characterised by long waiting times, particularly during peak hours.
These checkpoints slow the movement of Palestinians between villages, towns and cities, with delays often extending further depending on inspection procedures and conditions at the site, thereby creating major bottlenecks on routes used daily by thousands of Palestinians.
Attaf Abu Aliya, a taxi driver from the village of al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah, said he is forced to wait hours every day at checkpoints that soldiers frequently set up at the village entrance.
Under normal circumstances, the trip from al-Mughayyir to Ramallah takes only 30 minutes, but the tightened closure has turned the journey into an ordeal lasting many hours.

Araghchi to meet mediators in talks with US amid efforts to reopen Hormuz
Iran’s ISNA news agency reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and a delegation will meet with mediators involved in talks with the United States on Monday morning.
The latest proposals and views on the situation will be discussed during the talks, ISNA said.
A Qatari delegation has been in the United States and presented Washington with an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for economic relief.
Iran's Tasnim news agency said there were no plans for direct talks between Iranian and US officials.
The meetings come as Washington and Tehran continue to trade proposals over the strategic waterway amid increased tensions.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel shuts Palestinian shops to facilitate Jewish prayers in Jerusalem’s Old City
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Israel shuts Palestinian shops to facilitate Jewish prayers in Jerusalem’s Old City
Israeli forces have ordered dozens of Palestinian shops in the Old City of occupied East Jerusalem to close, restricting access to streets leading to the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The closure covers more than 50 shops and took effect on Sunday morning, the third day of the Sukkot holiday. It is due to remain in place until 2 October.
The shops are located in the Muslim Quarter, along streets leading to Bab al-Qattanin (Cotton Merchants' Gate), one of the main gates to Al-Aqsa used by Palestinian worshippers.
On Sunday night, hundreds of Israelis gathered in the area for holiday rituals.
Palestinian residents were ordered to remain indoors, while the Bab al-Qattanin leading to Al-Aqsa was closed.

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham walks onto the stage on the first day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool on 27 September (AFP)
Off
The Labour Party’s Conference Arrangements Committee (CAC) has blocked an emergency motion brought by party delegates on cancelling Palantir’s NHS contract over the company’s links to the Israeli military.
The motion, put forward at the party’s conference in Liverpool by the Labour-affiliated Socialist Health Association and at least three constituency parties, urged the government to cancel the £330m ($437m) contract to process NHS data with the controversial tech giant.
It said Palantir was “facing numerous allegations of involvement in serious breaches of human rights, including due to it developing technology for Israel's military to use in its unlawful occupation of Palestinian land and genocide in Gaza".
The motion said: "The Labour government has a responsibility to uphold public trust in politics, including in the awarding of public contracts, particularly where there are allegations of involvement in grave violations of international law."
But the Conference Arrangements Committee blocked the motion during the conference. Middle East Eye understands the CAC judged the motion did not meet the requisite criteria to be debated, but delegates and campaigners have questioned the decision.
Jon Byrne, a councillor from Hazel Grove Constituency Labour Party (CLP), one of the CLPs which submitted the motion, said in the conference hall on Monday morning: “I wish to question the CAC on its rejection of our emergency motion on Palantir’s NHS contracts, on the company’s involvement in the genocide in Gaza and on transparency on the control of decisions on contracts.

Iran does not fully control the Strait of Hormuz, US Central Command said, hitting back against claims from a senior Iranian military commander that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps “completely controls” the strategic waterway
In a post on X, Centcom said claims that “Iran has full control over the Strait of Hormuz … are false”. It added: “Iran has no navy because American forces sank it.”
According to Centcom, more than 1 billion barrels of oil have recently passed through the strait, demonstrating that Iran does not control the waterway.
American forces have been helping to keep commercial traffic flowing through the strait while enforcing a blockade on Iranian maritime trade, US officials have said previously.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran supreme leader says US will be forced out of Middle East
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Iran supreme leader says US will be forced out of Middle East
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Monday that the United States would be forced to leave the Middle East after suffering "painful blows", according to a statement carried by state television.
Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the start of the war in late February, made the remarks despite attempts to revive talks aimed at ending the fighting.
"Today, having suffered painful blows at the hands of valiant fighters and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they (the enemies) do not venture beyond the Arabian Sea," Khamenei said in the written statement attributed to him, without explicitly mentioning the United States.
"Whenever they have braved this risk, they have only brought harm upon themselves. It will not be long before the Arabian Sea, too, would rid itself of their presence," he added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian-American journalist freed after 13 days in Israeli detention
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Palestinian-American journalist freed after 13 days in Israeli detention
Palestinian-American journalist Naqaa Hamed was released from Damon Prison after 13 days, following an Israeli court decision.
Hamed was arrested on 15 September at the Tuqu checkpoint while returning from an assignment. She was separated from her camera crew and taken to an unknown location for questioning.
According to Israeli media, Hamed was arrested on suspicion of “cooperating with an enemy entity” and possible espionage. She had previously served as a correspondent for Iran’s Press TV in the occupied West Bank.
According to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society, 36 Palestinian journalists, including four women, remain detained in Israeli jails, along with about 90 Palestinian women.
